items.summary:
### Summary

Nuxt matches route rules against the request path with encoded slashes (`%2F`) left encoded, while the page router decodes them into route params. A request that spells a slash as `%2F` can therefore render a page through a catch-all route without the route rules configured for the path it resolves to. The fix for [GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp) deliberately left reserved escapes such as `%2F` encoded, so it did not cover this form.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass route rules that protect paths served by a catch-all page route, or by a custom route whose param can span several segments.

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/docs/internal/**': { appMiddleware: 'auth', headers: { 'X-Frame-Options': 'DENY' } },
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})
```

With `app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue`, `/docs/internal/guide` runs `auth`, but `/docs/internal%2Fguide` renders the same page without running `auth` and without the header. With a root `app/pages/[...slug].vue`, `/admin%2Fsecret` is rendered instead of redirected.

The rules skipped include server-side `redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr` and `noScripts`, and `appMiddleware`, `appLayout` and `redirect` as matched in the app during server rendering and client navigation. `getRouteRules` returns the same incomplete result.

Whether the page then shows protected content depends on how it reads the route:

- With a route such as `definePageMeta({ path: '/docs/:path(.*)' })`, `route.params.path` is `internal/guide` for both requests.
- With a repeatable catch-all (`[...slug].vue`), `route.params.slug` is `['internal/guide']` instead of `['internal', 'guide']`, so a page that joins the segments (`slug.join('/')`) to load content loads the protected resource.
- `route.path` keeps the encoding (`/docs/internal%2Fguide`), so a page that loads content by `route.path` does not resolve it.

Not affected:

- Static page routes and params that match a single segment. `/docs%2Finternal` does not match `app/pages/docs/internal.vue`.
- API handlers in `server/api` and `server/routes`. As far as we can tell, Nitro matches these against the same path as its route rules, so a handler and the rules for it agree.

Browsers send `%2F` in a path as written, so a plain link is enough to reach the page.

### Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.4`, together with `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4` and `@nuxt/vite-server@4.6.4`, which it depends on. Route rules are now resolved for both the request path and the path with each `%2F` read as a separator, and the rules matched by either apply. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

### Workarounds

Reject page requests whose path contains an encoded slash in a server middleware:

```ts
// server/middleware/encoded-slash.ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (/%2f/i.test(event.path.split('?')[0])) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404 })
  }
})
```

This also rejects legitimate uses, such as an API route that takes a scoped package name (`@scope%2Fname`) as a param; narrow the check to the path prefixes your route rules protect if you need those.

A reverse proxy or CDN that rejects or decodes encoded slashes before forwarding the request also removes the mismatch.

### Credits

Thanks to Riahi Foudhil for reporting this issue.

items.summary: ### Summary The fix for CVE-2026-46342 (GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v) binds each `/__nuxt_island/_.json` path to its props by hashing the `(name, props, context, source)` tuple. That hash was computed over `ohash`'s serialization, which does not escape quotes inside strings or delimiters inside keys, so two different prop objects can produce the same hash. A request with crafted props can therefore pass validation for another island's path and render different content at that path. ### Impact For example, these two prop objects serialize identically and share one island path: ```js { html: '', note: '' } { html: '\',note:\'' } ``` This reopens the scenarios described in GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v: - **`nuxt generate` / prerendering.** Nuxt caches prerendered island responses by path. If the crawler reaches a link to the colliding URL (for example in user-submitted content included in the build) before it renders the page that uses the legitimate props, the colliding response is written into the generated page. - **Path-keyed shared caches.** A CDN or reverse proxy that caches `/__nuxt_island/*` by path only, ignoring the query, can be primed with the colliding response. An attacker has to construct props that collide with a specific legitimate tuple, which in practice means at least part of that tuple is a string they control (for example a stored comment or profile field passed as a prop). Where a prop reaches an unsafe HTML sink in the island (`v-html`, `innerHTML`, a renderer treating a prop as HTML), the substituted response can execute script in the site's origin. Without such a sink, the impact is content substitution. Applications are not affected if they do not use server components or ``, or if no island receives attacker-influenced string props. Server-rendered responses that are not cached by path alone are also unaffected. ### Patches Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.4` and `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4`. The island hash is now computed over a canonical JSON encoding of the tuple, in which strings and keys are escaped, so different props can no longer produce the same hash. Island hashes change as a result. Clients that build island URLs themselves should use the exported `getIslandHash` rather than hashing with `ohash` directly. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to Nuxt 4. ### Workarounds - Ensure any intermediary cache keys `/__nuxt_island/*` on the full query string, not on the path alone. - Treat island props as untrusted input and do not pass them to `v-html` or other HTML sinks without sanitisation. - When prerendering, avoid including user-submitted links to `/__nuxt_island/` in crawled pages, for example by excluding that prefix with `nitro.prerender.ignore`: ```ts export default defineNuxtConfig({ nitro: { prerender: { ignore: [route => route.startsWith('/__nuxt_island/') && route.includes('?')], }, }, }) ``` ### Credits Thanks to rat5ak for reporting this issue.
items.title: Nuxt: Colliding island props can share one `/__nuxt_island` path (incomplete fix for CVE-2026-46342)

items.summary: The key agreements that protect a Wi-Fi connection rely on Diffie-Hellman, which a sufficiently capable quantum computer would break; an adversary can therefore record an association today and decrypt its traffic years later. Key establishment is thus the part of IEEE 802.11 that has to be migrated first. This work targets the two protocols that perform that agreement inside the frames used to set up the link: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), which encrypts otherwise open networks, and Fast Initial Link Setup (FILS), designed for fast connection in dense and mobile deployments. We propose replacing their Diffie-Hellman exchange with a hybrid one that runs the classical elliptic-curve agreement alongside ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and derives the master key from both secrets, so the connection stays protected as long as either component remains unbroken. The exchange reuses the frames each protocol already sends and adds no extra round trip; an access point can advertise the hybrid mode alongside classical OWE, and a station configured to require it refuses to associate without a completed post-quantum exchange. Binding the advertised capabilities to the derived key is specified as a design extension and is not part of the prototype. We validate the design with a working implementation on hostapd and wpa_supplicant: both endpoints derive the same key in every measured connection, with the two smaller parameter sets each enlarged association frame fits in a single frame even under a conservative 1500-byte fragmentation threshold, and the added connection time and computation stay below half a millisecond. The measurements are obtained on OWE; the design carries over to FILS, whose frame budget is left for specific measurement. Of the three ML-KEM parameter sets, the intermediate one offers the best balance between security level and size.
items.title: Post-Quantum Migration of Wi-Fi Key Establishment: A Hybrid ML-KEM Design for OWE and FILS, Validated on OWE with hostapd

items.summary: Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing. To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.
items.title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models

items.summary: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

items.summary: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights. The approach employs a general six-stage process with platform-specific adapters, utilizing either a PyTorch allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock to identify and read tensor allocations from video memory. We validate this acquisition on 33 open-source decoder-only models across nine architecture classes, demonstrating that the recovered bytes are byte-exact and usable for downstream analysis. As a use case, we apply linear probes trained on standard framework activations to the recovered states, successfully distinguishing refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88 on held-out prompts. This work establishes that live, observational access to intermediate hidden states is feasible on named inference platforms, providing a new source of evidence for examining the operational behavior of deployed AI systems.
items.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States

items.summary:
### Summary

LightSaml 5.0.0 (latest release; also confirmed on 4.6.1) validates an inbound `samlp:Response` by collecting its direct-child `saml:Assertion` elements and validating each one's `ds:Signature` via robrichards/xmlseclibs. The two layers disagree on which element a signature actually covers: LightSaml reads claims from the assertion node it collected, while xmlseclibs resolves the signed `Reference URI="#id"` with a document-wide `//*[@Id]` XPath that returns the first ID-bearing element anywhere in the document.

An attacker who has captured one genuine signed assertion can exploit this to surface attacker-authored, unsigned claims.

### Details

`Response::deserialize` collects assertions with `manyElementsFromXml`, whose relative XPath `saml:Assertion` matches only direct children of the `Response`. Each collected assertion is validated independently by `AssertionSignatureValidatorAction` against the out-of-band trusted IdP credential (resolved by Issuer entityId, never from the document):

https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/Protocol/Response.php#L122
https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/AbstractSamlModel.php#L93
https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Action/Assertion/Inbound/AssertionSignatureValidatorAction.php#L28

The check delegates to xmlseclibs `XMLSecurityDSig::validateReference()`, which first removes the signature node being validated from the shared document (enveloped-signature removal):

```php
if (! $docElem->isSameNode($this->sigNode)) {
    if ($this->sigNode->parentNode != null) {
        $this->sigNode->parentNode->removeChild($this->sigNode);   // strips sig from shared DOM
    }
}
```

https://github.com/robrichards/xmlseclibs/blob/3.1.5/src/XMLSecurityDSig.php#L596

`processRefNode()` then resolves `URI="#id"` document-wide and takes `item(0)`, the first ID-bearing element in the whole document, any name or namespace, not the one inside the signature's own subtree:

```php
$query = '//*['.$iDlist.']';
$dataObject = $xPath->query($query)->item(0);
```

https://github.com/robrichards/xmlseclibs/blob/3.1.5/src/XMLSecurityDSig.php#L525

So the digest target xmlseclibs picks (`//*[@Id]` item(0), anywhere) which isn't necessarily the one from the previous phase. LightSaml then reads claims (Subject/NameID, Conditions, Attributes) from the node it collected:

https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/Assertion/Assertion.php#L288

An example attacker buries the genuine signed bytes (the assertion with its `ds:Signature` element stripped) inside `samlp:Extensions`, so it is the first `@Id` element in document order but not a direct-child assertion. Present one forged direct-child assertion with the same `ID`, attacker claims, and a verbatim copy of the genuine `ds:Signature`:

```xml

                xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" ID="_resp" Version="2.0" IssueInstant="2024-01-01T00:00:00Z">
  <saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com</saml:Issuer>

  <!-- GENUINE signed bytes, buried in Extensions: first @Id document-wide (xmlseclibs picks this),
       but NOT a direct-child assertion (LightSaml ignores it). Signature element removed so the
       enveloped+exc-c14n digest target is the assertion sans Signature. -->
  <samlp:Extensions>
    <saml:Assertion ID="_signed_assertion" Version="2.0" IssueInstant="2024-01-01T00:00:00Z">
      <saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com</saml:Issuer>
      <saml:Subject><saml:NameID>alice@example.com</saml:NameID></saml:Subject>
      <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2024-01-01T00:00:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2099-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>

items.summary: Emerging quantum computers threaten to break the classical key exchange algorithms. To safeguard against these threats, migration to new quantum-safe algorithms is underway and expected to be expedited. Though resistant to attacks, the quantum safe algorithms may impact the real-world performance due to their large key lengths. In this work, we analyze the end-to-end performance of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol with the post-quantum (PQ) and hybrid cryptographic algorithms standardized by NIST. We develop a test setup to evaluate the performance of TLS connections between a client and a server under various network conditions. We focus on the impact of the new algorithms on the speed (throughput, connection time) and sustainability (energy, CPU cycles) of TLS 1.3. Our analysis demonstrates that the standardized post-quantum algorithms do not introduce any measurable performance degradations in TLS 1.3, despite their larger key lengths. However, hybrid algorithms introduce noticeable performance degradation, which becomes increasingly pronounced under adverse network conditions. Our analysis suggests that migration to hybrid algorithms should be ``network condition aware'' as poor network conditions can severely degrade performance in TLS 1.3. We provide anonymised link to the code and a web interface to analyse performance of various combination of algorithms.
items.title: PQC Migration: End-to-End Performance Profiling of Post Quantum Cryptographic Algorithms in mTLS

items.summary: The inheritance of crypto-assets faces a structural obstacle: ownership is the knowledge of a key, so the key either disappears with its owner or has to be shared beforehand. The Tales From the Crypt Protocol (TFCP) addressed one part of the problem, the distributed and privacy-preserving acknowledgment of a death by a blockchain. We revisit it with a new primitive. A \emph{baryonic key} is a physical object from which bits are obtained only through a measurement, are never stored digitally, and which exists in exactly $n$ copies, where $n$ is neither zero nor unbounded. We define the primitive, outline a candidate instantiation based on a replicated micro-fractured relief, and state its limits: digitising a copy is slow and tamper-evident, not impossible. We also outline other uses of the primitive, from post-quantum pre-shared keys to common coins for Byzantine agreement. We then give a threat model for TFCP, review the attack models of the literature that apply to it, and show where it resists and where it does not. We propose TFCP-B, in which decrypting the will requires both a secret shared among registrars and the response of a baryonic key, and in which heirs claim their share through hash commitments, without any prior key or wallet. We detail each change from TFCP to TFCP-B, with its rationale and its price. TFCP-B removes the anonymity loss caused by colluding registrars and blocks several false-alarm attacks. It does not remove the shallow-account attack, remains exposed to transaction censorship during the deliberation period, and introduces new assumptions on custodians and reading devices. The security arguments are informal and the physical figures are design estimates.
items.title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol

items.summary: An enterprise breach causes most of its damage after the perimeter is crossed. Once an attacker gains a foothold, they can move laterally to other hosts, take over the trusted services of the network, and encrypt the backups needed for recovery. Defenders, on the other hand, need to study this post-compromise stage, but they cannot rehearse it on a production enterprise network. Building such an enterprise network manually is time-consuming, and resetting it to its clean state between runs is still harder. As a result, security experiments are difficult to perform, compare and reproduce. We develop Enterprise Network Testbed for Reproducible Attack and Defense Practices (ENTRAP), an Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) cyber range that defines a fully segmented enterprise as version-controlled automation. ENTRAP uses Ansible, KVM/Libvirt, and Cloud-init to provision the environment and reset it to a clean state whenever necessary. The enterprise network includes several entities such as a gateway, an internal Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), DNS, DHCP, a backup server, a web server, and clients. On this network, a user can learn to assemble the entities, launch attacks, and write rules or defensive measures that harden its security. We launch three attacks: a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS)-backed ransomware campaign, a Layer-2 DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP attack, and perimeter web exploitation. Each attack runs from a clean state, and ENTRAP acts as a reproducible generator of labeled attack datasets. Using the collected dataset, we train a Random Forest classifier for ransomware detection and present its evaluation results. We publicly release the codebase, collected logs, and datasets to facilitate further research.
items.title: Experience: ENTRAP - An IaC Enterprise Cyber Range for Reproducible Security Assessment and Dataset Generation

items.summary: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.

items.summary: Oracle attacks show the importance of a correct implementation of cryptographic standards when translated into code. A notable example is the Bleichenbacher attack on RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and all the improvements that have been suggested over the decades. This paper shows how an attacker knowing a few least significant bytes of an RSA message can take advantage of a server with an oracle side-channel to decrypt the full message bit by bit. We will consider two oracles that can be tested with chosen ciphertexts: one revealing whether the decrypted message starts with the 00 02 bytes and a second one revealing if the decrypted message is fully PKCS compliant. For an attacker knowing the three least significant bytes of the message, the first oracle provides an attack where one oracle call gives the next least significant bit of the message and the second an attack which requires, with high probability, a small constant number of oracle calls to the oracle, with a constant which depends on the length of the message and the desired probability of success. The attack divides the message bits into two sections, one with the known part and one with the unknown part, and then chooses transformations that will keep the unknown part, except for the last unknown bit, orders of magnitude below the integer coming from the known part. The resulting string either gives a valid padding or not depending on the value of the unknown bit. The attacker can minimize the number of oracle calls at the cost of some local computation. Finally, the same method is adapted to show how it can also be used to extract the few least significant bytes of the message with an increased cost where the main complexity is finding a second valid message with a correct padding starting from the original captured ciphertext.
items.title: A Bleichenbacher bit-by-bit oracle attack from partial message knowledge

items.summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
items.title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems

On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

items.summary: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.
items.title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents

items.summary: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.
items.title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection

items.summary: Synthetic text, images, and video are rising. Software-only detectors are power-hungry, too slow, and costly, and do not scale with demand. When software cannot scale, historically hardware often comes to the rescue. We perform the first reverse engineering of a compression accelerator--Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) microarchitecture and--find different amount of time on each, a novel data structure-dependent property. Using this information, we then build Lasso, a low-cost, high-performance detector for AI-generated content that turns the accelerator into a measuring instrument. For text detection, Lasso achieves 100% accuracy on original DetectRL text and retains 92% average accuracy after paraphrasing, compared with 78% for Binoculars and 55% for DetectGPT. Across original, paraphrased, and perturbed text, it achieves 82% average accuracy, outperforming all five baselines. With topic, length, and formatting matched, accuracy reaches 95% for instruction-tuned generators, including when the tested generator is unseen. On RAID, accuracy averages 82% when trained on one generator and tested on another, and 74% across eight held-out domains. Detection takes 0.74 microseconds, a speedup of at least 83,784x across five baselines. At the same time, Lasso consumes over 99% less energy per document than both Binoculars and DetectGPT. At the same time, Lasso detects AI-generated videos, software code, and images with 67.5%, 70% and 78% accuracy, respectively, with low latency and power opening avenues for practical real time and edge device detection of multimodality AI artifacts for the first time. No other compared technique supports detection across all four modalities: text, video, images, and code.
items.title: Lasso: Towards Sustainable AI-Generated Media Detection with Intel QAT On-Chip Compression

items.summary: The CubeSat Space Protocol (CSP) is widely used for communication in CubeSat missions, yet its security model and attack surface remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present a systematic security analysis of CSP and identify fundamental limitations in its trust assumptions, coarse-grained network abstractions, privileged management services, application command semantics, and lack of mission-context awareness. Based on these findings, we develop a taxonomy of CSP attacks spanning four classes: network identity abuse, management service abuse, application semantic abuse, and mission context abuse. We then introduce Stargate, a modular, mission-aware firewall that enforces CSP-specific policies derived from this taxonomy, including node and service authorization, command-level filtering, and mission-context constraints. We implement Stargate and evaluate it on a virtual testbed based on a real-world CubeSat mission and flight software. Stargate successfully blocks all 11 representative attacks across the four attack classes while introducing only 1.42 ms of additional median round-trip latency. Our results demonstrate that protocol- and mission-aware policy enforcement provides a practical approach for securing CSP-based spacecraft networks.
items.title: Stargate: Security Analysis and Mission-Aware Firewall for the CubeSat Space Protocol

items.summary: We consider a physical layer authentication scenario in which a legitimate user (Alice) communicates with an authenticator (Bob) through a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), controlled by Bob. An attacker (Trudy) aims to impersonate Alice by suitably precoding her messages and still transmitting them through the RIS. This two-part study analyzes this attack-defense interaction between Bob and Trudy under perfect (Part I) and partial (Part II) channel knowledge by all the agents. Part I formulates the joint RIS selection and precoder design under perfect channel knowledge as a finite zero-sum game, establishing exact channel subspace conditions for attack indistinguishability alongside equilibrium mixed strategies. Part II extends the defense to incomplete channel information, where each agent observes only its own channel, by formulating a finite-action Bayesian game and characterizing the resulting Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Simulations in geometric and 3GPP TR 38.901 UMi-NLOS channels reveal that authentication performance is governed by available spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and operating signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equilibrium strategies effectively balance communication rate and security, outperforming conventional benchmark policies.
items.title: Game-Theoretic Analysis of RIS-Assisted Challenge-Response PLA - Part II: Partial Channel Knowledge

nvmet-tcp: check INIT_FAILED before nvmet_req_uninit in digest error path

In nvmet_tcp_try_recv_ddgst(), when a data digest mismatch is detected,

had returned false and percpu_ref_tryget_live() was never executed. The
unconditional percpu_ref_put() inside nvmet_req_uninit() then causes a
refcount underflow, leading to a WARNING in

eventually a permanent workqueue deadlock.

nvmet_req_uninit(), matching the existing pattern in
nvmet_tcp_execute_request().

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmet-tcp: Fix potential UAF when ddgst mismatch

Shivam Kumar found via vulnerability testing:
When data digest is enabled on an NVMe/TCP connection and a digest
mismatch occurs on a non-final H2C_DATA PDU during an R2T-based
data transfer, the digest error handler in nvmet_tcp_try_recv_ddgst()
calls nvmet_req_uninit() — which performs percpu_ref_put() on the
submission queue — but does NOT mark the command as completed. It
does not set cqe->status, does not modify rbytes_done, and does not
clear any flag. When the subsequent fatal error triggers queue
teardown, nvmet_tcp_uninit_data_in_cmds() iterates all commands,
checks nvmet_tcp_need_data_in() for each one, and finds that the
already-uninited command still appears to need data (because
rbytes_done < transfer_len and cqe->status == 0). It therefore calls
nvmet_req_uninit() a second time on the same command — a double
percpu_ref_put against a single percpu_ref_get.

items.summary:
The Zephyr WebSocket client validates the server's handshake response in on_header_value() in subsys/net/lib/websocket/websocket.c. The comparison was performed as strncmp(at, str, length), where length is the length of the value the server sent rather than the length of the expected value, so the check only asked whether the received value was a prefix of the expected base64(SHA-1(key || GUID)). A server that returned a handful of correct characters passed, and a response carrying an empty Sec-WebSocket-Accept: header caused strncmp() to be called with a count of zero, which returns 0 and set ctx->sec_accept_ok with no comparison performed at all. The header-value callback also cleared ctx->sec_accept_present after the first chunk, so a value split across receive-buffer boundaries was only ever examined in part.

ctx->sec_accept_ok is the sole WebSocket-specific gate in websocket_connect(); the client does not check the HTTP status code or the Upgrade:/Connection: headers. Any HTTP response containing an empty or prefix-matching Sec-WebSocket-Accept header therefore completed the handshake, after which the socket is finalized as a WebSocket and all further peer bytes are parsed as frames. The affected path is driven directly by remote input through subsys/net/lib/http/http_parser.c, and is reached by every user of websocket_connect(), including MQTT over WebSocket (subsys/net/lib/mqtt/mqtt_transport_websocket.c) and subsys/net/lib/ocpp/ocpp.c.

The Sec-WebSocket-Accept exchange is not a secret-based authentication -- an endpoint or on-path attacker that sees the request can compute the expected value -- so the impact is bounded to parties that never observed the handshake request: a caching or transparent intermediary replaying a canned response, an off-path attacker injecting a spoofed response, or a non-WebSocket endpoint the client was induced to talk to. For those, the per-connection binding that RFC 6455 requires the client to enforce provided no protection at all, letting a single crafted response convince the device it holds a live WebSocket session and causing it to send application data to, and accept frames from, an unverified peer. There is no memory-safety consequence.

The fix compares each delivered chunk against the expected value at the position reached so far, refuses a chunk that would overrun it, and accepts only once every byte of the expected value -- and no more -- has been matched; on_header_field() now also clears the flag for any other header so a partial value cannot be continued across an intervening header.

items.summary:
The Synopsys DesignWare I3C controller driver (drivers/i3c/i3c_dw.c) tracks free Device Address Table (DAT) slots with get_free_pos(), which signals an exhausted table by returning -1. The helper declared its return type as uint8_t, so the sentinel was truncated to 255, and both consumers (dw_i3c_attach_device() and dw_i3c_i2c_attach_device()) also stored it in a uint8_t before testing if (pos < 0) — a comparison that is never true for an unsigned value. The exhaustion guard was therefore inert in every build.

With the guard defeated, an attach attempted on a full DAT proceeds with pos == 255: it writes data->dw_i3c_i2c_priv_data[255].id, more than 200 bytes past the end of the 32-element dw_i3c_i2c_priv_data array and past the end of struct dw_i3c_data; it stores the resulting out-of-bounds address in desc->controller_priv, from which later detach, reattach and IBI operations read the slot index back; and it performs a 32-bit MMIO store 1020 bytes beyond the hardware DAT base, outside the table the controller reports. The attach still returns success, so the upper layer believes the device is bound.

The DAT is smaller than the software array (its depth is read from DEVICE_ADDR_TABLE_POINTER, commonly 8 or 16 entries), so exhaustion is reachable. In a dual-role build (CONFIG_I3C_DUAL_ROLE with CONFIG_I3C_USE_IBI) acting as a secondary controller, the attach count is supplied by the bus's active controller: i3c_sec_handoffed() attaches one device per entry of the received DEFTGTS list, so a hostile or malfunctioning controller on the local I3C bus that declares more targets than the local DAT depth triggers the condition once per surplus entry. Exhaustion can also be reached from a devicetree that declares more devices than the table holds, or by repeated i3c attach shell commands.

Impact is bounded: the out-of-bounds store is a single byte of fixed value at a fixed displacement, with no attacker-chosen data or offset, so the realistic outcomes are corruption of neighbouring static driver state, writes into reserved controller registers, and inconsistent driver bookkeeping (a crash or a wedged I3C bus) rather than a controllable memory-write primitive. The attack vector is the local chip-to-chip I3C bus; there is no network-reachable path.

items.summary:
The Bluetooth Classic SDP server in subsys/bluetooth/host/classic/sdp.c allocated every response PDU through bt_sdp_create_pdu(), which expands to bt_l2cap_create_pdu() and therefore uses a K_FOREVER timeout. The allocation is made from sdp_pool, a fixed pool holding only CONFIG_BT_MAX_CONN buffers (one in the default configuration) that is shared with the SDP client role. When the pool is empty the call blocks without a bound.

The allocation is reached from bt_sdp_recv() on the Bluetooth host's RX context: the bt_workq "BT RX WQ" workqueue in the default configuration since v3.1.0, and the dedicated "BT RX" thread before that. This context processes all normal-priority HCI events and all received ACL data. The SDP L2CAP server is registered on PSM 0x0001 with no security requirement (BT_SECURITY_L0), so an unpaired, unauthenticated BR/EDR peer within radio range of a connectable device can drive it. Every malformed or unrecognised SDP PDU reaches send_err_rsp(), and the sdp_svc_search_req(), sdp_svc_att_req() and sdp_svc_search_att_req() handlers allocate as well, so a short burst of pipelined requests drains the pool and parks the RX context in the blocking allocation.

A pool buffer is released only once its response has been sent, and a peer that withholds baseband acknowledgements keeps the controller's buffers for the link full, so the response is never sent. While the RX context is blocked, the entire Bluetooth host, for all connections and both LE and BR/EDR, stops processing normal-priority HCI events and received data. In most affected releases the stall is permanent. Queued PDUs are freed only by connection or channel teardown, which waits for the normal-priority Disconnection Complete handler, and that handler runs on the blocked RX context, so the host does not recover without a reset. In v3.7.0 through v4.1.x the TX processor discards the queued response once the link supervision timeout drops the connection, so each stall ends at that timeout, but the peer can reconnect and repeat it for as long as it stays in range. The impact is limited to availability; no memory corruption or information disclosure is involved.

The fix adds sdp_svc_create_pdu() using K_NO_WAIT, pre-allocates the response buffer once in bt_sdp_recv(), stashes the request in sdp->recv_pending when no buffer is available, and retries it from a work handler once a buffer is freed by the pool destroy callback.

items.summary: Faust.js is a headless WordPress toolkit. Prior to 1.8.12, the FaustWP generateAuthorizationCode GraphQL mutation called wp_authenticate_username_password and wp_authenticate_email_password directly instead of using wp_authenticate. This bypassed callbacks registered on WordPress's outer authenticate filter, including policies for multifactor authentication, single sign-on, IP allowlists, or disabled accounts. On a site using FaustWP local login and one of those policies, an attacker with a valid username or email and password could obtain an authorization code and exchange it through /api/faust/auth/token for access and refresh tokens even when the normal WordPress login path would deny access. This issue is fixed in version 1.8.12.

Server and reverse-proxy logs, browser history, and shared caches can retain sensitive filters, marking-restricted identifiers, and investigation search arguments, allowing a person with access to those records to recover legitimate users' query contents. GraphQL mutations are not accepted over GET, and the issue does not permit code execution. This issue is fixed in version 7.260722.0.

Prior to 7.260706.0, the logsWorkerConfig GraphQL query is authorized with the broad CONNECTORAPI capability and returns Elasticsearch connection details including elasticsearch_username, elasticsearch_password, elasticsearch_api_key, the URL, index, proxy, and TLS-verification setting. A holder of any connector API bearer token can retrieve this credential material. If the returned credentials are valid and Elasticsearch is reachable, the caller can directly read, modify, or delete OpenCTI indices and audit history outside application-layer role, marking, organization, and audit controls, with the practical impact bounded by the credentials' privileges and network reachability. This issue is fixed in version 7.260706.0.

Prior to 7.260624.0, an Organization Administrator with VIRTUAL_ORGANIZATION_ADMIN and KNOWLEDGE_KNUPDATE can use organizationFieldPatch to replace the administered organization's grantable_groups without a SETTINGS_SETACCESSES authorization check. The administrator can add the built-in Administrators group to that grant scope and then bypass the grantable_groups guard added by the incomplete CVE-2026-44730 remediation to add their own account to Administrators. Membership grants the BYPASS capability after session cache refresh, escalating the tenant-scoped account to global administrator with access across organizations, users, settings, markings, connectors, and ingestion. This issue is fixed in version 7.260624.0.

items.summary: OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260416.0, public TAXII 2.1 collections configured with taxii_public set to true are served under the high-privilege SYSTEM_USER context rather than a restricted public-sharing user context. Unauthenticated requests can therefore bypass object markings, organization segregation, and authorized_members restrictions and retrieve restricted threat-intelligence objects that match the collection filters; a broad or absent filter can expose most of the database. Version 7.260416.0 remediates this issue for new configurations, but public-sharing configurations created before that version are not covered and are tracked separately in GHSA-25r9-q6rp-j7jw.

items.summary:
In Eclipse BaSyx Go Components versions up to and including 1.1.3, ABAC-enabled deployments match `ROUTE` access rules against the fully decoded request path, while the router routes on the raw, still encoded path. An encoded slash (`%2F`) inside a path value is a segment separator for the access check but part of the value for the router, so a request can match a narrow `ROUTE` rule while the handler returns a different, larger resource.



An authenticated caller whose rules grant READ only on parts of a resource can therefore read the whole resource. In the DPP API, a rule such as `/v1/dpps/*/elements/*`, meant to grant only passport elements, also grants the complete passport whose identifier contains `/elements/`. In the Submodel Repository, AAS Repository and AAS Environment, a rule such as `/submodels/*/submodel-elements/*/attachment`, meant to grant only file attachments, also grants the complete element whose stored idShort contains `%2F`.



The issue is fixed in Eclipse BaSyx Go Components v1.1.4.

items.summary:
Authentication bypass by spoofing vulnerability in Apache APISIX.



On routes using jwe-decrypt with strict: false and a
forward_header distinct from the token header an unauthenticated
client can supply the value the upstream treats as gateway-decrypted
plaintext. Similar can happen when forward-auth is configured with allow_degradation: true, and the auth service is unavailable.



This issue affects Apache APISIX: from 3.18.0 through 3.19.0.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.20.0, which fixes the issue.

Prior to versions 3.3.10, 4.25.1, and 4.28.0, CRS rules in the 921 (protocol-attack), 930 (LFI), 931 (RFI), 932 (RCE), 933 (PHP), 934 (generic), 941 (XSS), 942 (SQLi), and 943 (session-fixation) families inspect XML request bodies via the XPath expression XML:/*. That expression matches only element text nodes — it does not match XML attribute values. As a result, an attacker who places an attack payload inside an XML attribute (e.g. or ) bypasses CRS detection entirely. This is verified empirically against a local CRS test instance and against the public CRS sandbox. The bypass affects approximately 159 rules across 9 rule files and applies at every paranoia level (PL1 through PL4), since the variable list is more or less shared across PLs. The 944 (Java) family is the only one that correctly includes XML://@* in addition to XML:/* and is therefore unaffected. This issue has been patched in versions 3.3.10, 4.25.1, and 4.28.0.

items.summary: A cleartext storage flaw was found in the AAP Gateway Operator. When reconciling an AutomationController, the operator reads the protected resource-server Secret (Secret/<aap-name>-resource-server, key controller_resource_server_secret) and copies its plaintext value into the generated AutomationController custom resource under spec.extra_settings (RESOURCE_SERVER.SECRET_KEY). Although the operator uses no_log to keep the value out of its own logs, serializing it into the custom resource exposes it to any principal able to read the AutomationController CR without permission to read the backing Kubernetes Secret, breaking the expected OpenShift RBAC separation between the two resources. The value may also propagate into Kubernetes API/etcd storage, GitOps and Argo diffs and history, rendered manifests, support bundles, and audit data. The resource-server secret is intended for trusted Gateway-to-Controller service authentication, and its disclosure may allow a user to impersonate a trusted Controller service and reach privileged service-index APIs.

items.summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.
items.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.
items.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents

items.summary: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. items.summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.
items.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models

items.summary: Malware detection needs scores calibrated at a fixed false positive rate (FPR) and decisions an analyst can read: feature-based detectors give the first, large language models (LLMs) on decompiled code the second, through generated text of uncalibrated confidence. System One decision models answer a typed question about a text with a probability over its declared answers in one forward pass. We present the first evaluation of these models for Windows Portable Executable malware detection, analyze how they decide, and propose S1Mal, an ensemble on the typed answers and the embedding of CLM-8B. In an isolated virtual machine, Ghidra and capa decompose each binary, and the host renders the records into a canonical textual state, a digest of headers, imports, MITRE ATT&CK capabilities and strings, optionally with decompiled functions, without class shortcuts. Three readouts score each model on the state: A0, the probability of one verdict question; A1, 32 atomic behavioral questions weighed by gradient-boosted trees; A2, heads on the model's state embedding. S1Mal feeds gradient-boosted trees with the atomic answers and the A2 score of CLM-8B. We evaluate CLM-8B, ten open decision models and two LLMs read through logits on BODMAS temporal splits, SOREL-20M out-of-distribution malware and 14,534 matched benign files. On BODMAS, A0 wastes the static evidence: its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) spans 0.4025-0.8590 across 13 models. A1 recovers it, raising every model's AUROC by +54.61% on average; A2 lifts CLM-8B by +0.2749 to 0.9943, above a combiner on digest facts (0.9901), and reaches 0.9853-0.9948 on nine open models. S1Mal reaches 0.9946 and detects 93.47% of the malware at a realized FPR of 1.45%, and 59.15% at 0.1% FPR on the test ROC curve, against 46.59% with A2. S1Mal gives analysts calibrated decisions, each with the atomic answers behind it.
items.title: A First Look at System One Decision Models for Malware Detection

items.summary: Tamarin-based formal verification of security protocols requires expert-authored multiset rewriting rules and temporal-logic lemmas. Translating a natural-language protocol description into a complete formal model with an LLM is hard because syntactic, reachability, and property-level errors compound across the multi-step modeling process, and a single agent that both authors and self-evaluates cannot reliably localize them. We present MASTA, a multi-agent system that addresses these difficulties through three innovations. First, an operational--evaluative role decomposition assigns rule modeling to an Architect, property modeling to an Auditor, and pure dispatch to a dedicated Arbiter that holds no authoring duties. Second, the Arbiter implements a Tamarin-anchored scheduler that dispatches the next agent based on the latest verifier verdict and routes problem-tagged fixes through a modification list, with a six-class problem taxonomy and an LLM deduplication check preventing routing deadlock. Third, we construct a benchmark of 10 protocols paired with 139 mutation variants and five fine-grained metrics that jointly assess model correctness ($M_1$--$M_3$) and completeness ($M_4$--$M_5$). On this benchmark, MASTA on Qwen 3.5-plus improves over OpenCode on the same backbone by up to $+0.27$ on individual metrics and ranks first on both the correctness and completeness averages, surpassing Codex (GPT-5.5) and Claude Code (Opus 4.7) despite using a weaker LLM. Ablations on five protocols confirm that removing the Arbiter collapses property and verification scores to zero.
items.title: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/qianli-wang/ReconPotBench
items.title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance

items.summary: Replaying a vulnerability's original proof-of-concept after patching tests whether its reported trigger remains reproducible, but does not establish that the underlying security invariant holds on other code paths. We present a benign, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study across four LLM agent frameworks and four invariant classes. For PraisonAI, we compare original-trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M). We also perform five before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI. Each run reports VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE, gated by a positive authorized control. Probes use inert markers or builtins-reachability checks. At PraisonAI 4.6.31, the original tool-loading trigger is blocked while the tool_override path still violates the invariant. This reproduces the publicly documented CVE-2026-44334 bypass of CVE-2026-40287; neither tested path shows a violation at 4.6.32. For CrewAI, we observe a violation in tested release 1.11.0 and confinement in 1.11.1, without claiming the earliest fixed release. Fourteen harness-validation scenarios produced their expected verdicts. Only one same-version B0-versus-M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probes invoke loader functions directly and establish boundary behavior under the supplied setup, not a full end-to-end exploit. A non-violation verdict applies only to the tested probe, version, and configuration and is not a proof of safety. This pilot reconstructs a known incomplete fix; it neither introduces a new testing technique nor estimates vulnerability prevalence.
items.title: Beyond the Patch: Reconstructing an Incomplete-Fix Patch Bypass in LLM Agent Frameworks with Control-Gated, Benign Probes

items.summary: LLM serving engines cache prompt prefixes; a cache hit skips computation and returns faster, so a shared cache reveals whether others have sent a given text. Per-account salting closes this channel but forgoes cross-tenant reuse and isolates only whole accounts, even where access is redistributed or trust domains are subdivided below them. Defenses that share globally but hide hits promise reuse without relying on account boundaries. Hiding a hit requires everything tenants observe afterwards to be distributed as if it had missed. The defenses we examine target the hit-miss gap; we instead follow where the saved time goes. Step-based schedulers that never idle while work waits pass it in full to every request queued behind the hit, shifting each earlier by the same amount. An attacker within ordinary rate limits brackets a probe with two groups of listeners that each return one token, sends them in one short burst, and counts in how many steps they finish. Replaying a production trace on one vLLM instance at up to half capacity, a single probe detects cached texts of 256 tokens or more with advantage at least 0.98. Hiding only the hit request falls to one probe on vLLM and SGLang; random delays must reach about ten times the shift or more to cut the advantage to 0.1; narrowing what is shared gives no guarantee against this inference. Since any observable tenant benefit is also a signal, we prove that a rate-limited tenant's gain from content written by k other accounts is at most of order k times the leakage allowed, whatever the provider does with identities; at zero leakage, only the provider keeps the savings. Exact hiding is attainable in principle on one instance, but mechanisms that only pause or hold work know skipped work's duration only approximately, so under saturated prefill they must pad every step that may hold a hit, at a price that grows with time rather than with hits.
items.title: Where the Savings Go: The Limits of Hiding Cross-Tenant Cache Hits in LLM Serving

items.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems, from clinical information retrieval to workflow automation and decision support, which introduces new security, privacy, and trust risks with direct implications for patient care. While prior work has examined these risks from technical and regulatory perspectives, less is known about how these risks are naturally discussed in online communities. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 14 medical communities on Reddit and extract 6,514 relevant posts. Through systematic qualitative coding and LLM-assisted classification, we investigate concerns expressed in healthcare AI discussions, their prevalence, and how they evolve over time. Our analysis reveals that users perceive healthcare AI as expanding traditional healthcare trust boundaries and attack surfaces through integrations with electronic health records, third-party services, cloud platforms, and automated clinical workflows. Posts express concerns about over-privileged access to sensitive records, opaque data flows, unauthorized secondary use, and unsafe automation can amplify the consequences of errors and misuse. We identify four attitudes toward these risks: exploring questions of accountability and harm, cautiously accepting AI with stronger safeguards, skepticism about system trustworthiness, and resignation to growing data exposure and automation. Longitudinal analysis shows that SP&T discussions have increased significantly, with shifts coinciding with major healthcare AI deployments, privacy incidents, and regulatory developments. These findings illuminate changing trust relationships and data-governance challenges, informing the design and governance of safer, more transparent, and accountable healthcare AI systems.
items.title: Understanding Users' Security, Privacy, and Trust Concerns in Healthcare AI Systems

items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.
items.title: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding and Repairing Risky Fallback in LLM Agents

items.summary: Software vulnerabilities persist as a critical threat despite the deployment of sophisticated detection tools and AI assistants. While detection has advanced, the subsequent code repair phase remains a primary bottleneck; manual intervention is inherently slow, costly, and prone to introducing secondary regressions and issues. In this paper, we investigate whether an iterative, LLM-based pipeline can provide a robust solution for the automated repair of vulnerable functions in real-world code. We propose a generalized framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) through a multi-stage feedback loop. We benchmark this approach against state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash, demonstrating that such a pipeline can achieve high-quality code repair. To support the broader security community, we provide our evaluation framework, fine-tuned weights, and comprehensive experimental dataset on our website: https://sites.google.com/view/llm4cve
items.title: Found, but Not Fixed : From Software Vulnerability Discovery to Fixes with Iterative LLM Pipelines

items.summary: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.
items.title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming

items.summary: Enterprise information is commonly stored across multiple platforms rather than in one centralized location. Answering questions about workplace activities may require information from several sources, including project documents, task management systems, and team conversations. Therefore, we evaluate Orbit AI, a tool-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that uses a ReAct agent implemented with LangGraph to retrieve and combine information from three different workspace sources. We compare three configurations: (1) a standalone LLM without retrieval, (2) document-based RAG, and (3) a multi-tool agent with access to all three sources. The held-out evaluation set contains 80 questions designed for Phase 3 workspace; Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite achieves an accuracy of 86.25% with the complete agent. Document-only RAG achieves 60.00% (26.25 pp higher), and the plain LLM achieves 23.13%. For multi-source questions, the full agent answers 84.38%, while document-only RAG answers 40.63%, a 43.75 pp increase. The evaluated Llama 3.2 configuration with local inference achieves 5.50% overall correctness under rubric v2.2. The Llama 3.2 full-agent configuration achieves a held-out accuracy of 52.50%, which is 1.88 pp higher than the accuracy of document-only RAG. The gain of Gemini is equivalent to 26.25 pp. The comparison must be taken with a pinch of salt, because Gemini was accessed via an API hosted by them, while Llama was run locally via Ollama and the models are of different size. It is therefore not possible to isolate the cause of the performance gaps in this experiment. The paper also addresses the constraints of the evaluation such as the small artificial workspace and the similarity of the Q53 problem to a problem in the system prompt.
items.title: Orbit AI: Evaluating Tool-Augmented Agents For Enterprise Question Answering

items.summary: Watermarking has emerged as an important technique for distinguishing AI-generated text from human-written text. However, most existing work is primarily empirical, relies on ad hoc watermarking designs, and lacks a fundamental understanding of the performance limits. In this paper, we propose a unified theoretical framework for statistical watermarking of large language models (LLMs), casting the problem as an independence test between generated text and common randomness and jointly designing the watermarking embedder and the detector. Our objective is to maximize detection power while controlling the worst-case false positive rate (FPR) and limiting distortion to text quality. A central focus of our framework is the design of the common randomness, which plays a critical role in both watermark embedding and detection. We characterize the fundamental limits of statistical watermarking under both fixed and optimizable common randomness. Our results show that optimizing the common randomness does not improve the fundamental limits: the best achievable performance is the same as that with fixed common randomness. Nevertheless, common randomness design remains highly important because it can substantially simplify detector design. In particular, with optimizable common randomness, a fixed, deterministic, and model-agnostic detector can achieve optimal performance. We further study a practical setting with fixed uniform common randomness and a fixed deterministic detector, and characterize its performance gap relative to the optimizable case, thereby demonstrating the practical value of optimizable common randomness.
items.title: Fundamental Limits of Statistical Watermarking for LLMs with Fixed and Optimizable Common Randomness
